title: Catalogs and interoperability
summary: What an Iceberg catalog does, how the main catalog implementations differ, and how to let several engines share tables safely.

blocks.text: Chapter 22 showed that an Iceberg commit is a compare-and-swap of one pointer. The component that holds that pointer is the **catalog**. It looks like plumbing, but it decides which engines can use your tables, how commits stay atomic, who is allowed to read and write, and how hard it is to migrate later.
24.1 What a catalog is responsible for

items: **Name resolution**: map `namespace.table` to the location of the current metadata file.
**Atomic commits**: implement the compare-and-swap so two writers cannot both win.
**Namespace operations**: create, list, rename and drop tables and namespaces.
**Access control and credentials** (in modern catalogs): decide who may read or write, and hand out storage credentials scoped to one table.

blocks.text: Everything else (schemas, snapshots, statistics) lives in the metadata files, which is why two catalogs pointing at the same metadata file see the same table. It is also why registering one table in two catalogs is dangerous: each catalog accepts commits independently, the pointers diverge, and one catalog's commits silently disappear from the other's view.
One table, one catalog of record. Other systems may *mirror* or *federate* it read-only, but exactly one catalog must accept commits. Violating this is the most common cause of 'lost' Iceberg data.

blocks.text: 24.3 The REST catalog specification

Older catalogs required every engine to ship a client for every backend. The Iceberg REST catalog spec, an OpenAPI definition maintained by the Iceberg project, inverts this: engines implement one HTTP protocol, and any server implementing it becomes usable from Spark, Trino, Flink, PyIceberg, DuckDB, Snowflake and others.

A commit is sent as a list of **requirements** (for example 'table UUID is X', 'ref main currently points at snapshot S') and **updates** (add snapshot, set ref, add schema). The server checks the requirements and applies the updates atomically, so the compare-and-swap happens on the server, where it can also enforce permissions, validate changes and emit audit events. The spec also defines optional endpoints such as multi-table transactions; servers differ in what they implement.

blocks.title: Engine access through a REST catalog with credential vending

blocks.text: Credential vending

Without vending, every engine needs broad IAM access to the bucket, so authorization effectively happens at the storage layer and table-level grants in the catalog are advisory. With vending, the client asks the catalog for access (signalled with the `X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation` header), the catalog checks the caller's privileges on that table, and returns short-lived storage credentials limited to the table's location (or offers remote signing of requests). The engine then needs no standing storage permissions at all.
24.4 Catalog products

items: **Apache Polaris**: an open-source implementation of the REST spec, originally contributed by Snowflake. It has internal catalogs (Polaris owns commits) and external catalogs (mirrors of tables managed elsewhere, read-only through Polaris), principals, principal roles and catalog roles with fine-grained privileges, and credential vending.
**Snowflake Open Catalog**: Snowflake's managed service based on Polaris. Snowflake can sync its own managed Iceberg tables into it so external engines can read them (chapter 28).

**Project Nessie**: a transactional catalog with Git-like semantics across *many* tables: branches, commits and merges at catalog level, so a multi-table change can be published atomically. Exposes the REST API as well as its own.

**Unity Catalog**: Databricks' governance catalog, also available as open source. It can expose tables to Iceberg clients through an Iceberg REST endpoint and is extending native Iceberg support; check the current documentation for which operations external engines may perform.
**Cloud-native options**: AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables (managed Iceberg tables with built-in maintenance), Google BigLake metastore and others. Capabilities evolve quickly.

blocks.text: Catalog features change faster than almost anything else in this trail. Treat any feature matrix, including the ones in this chapter, as a starting point and verify against current documentation before committing to a design.
24.5 Multi-engine access in practice
The promise of Iceberg is one copy of data used by several engines. In practice each engine is configured to talk to the same catalog. Spark, for example:

blocks.title: Spark properties for a REST catalog (values illustrative)
blocks.text:
spark.sql.extensions=org.apache.iceberg.spark.extensions.IcebergSparkSessionExtensions
spark.sql.catalog.lake=org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog
spark.sql.catalog.lake.type=rest
spark.sql.catalog.lake.uri=https://catalog.example.internal/api/catalog
spark.sql.catalog.lake.warehouse=analytics
spark.sql.catalog.lake.credential=<client-id>:<client-secret>
spark.sql.catalog.lake.header.X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation=vended-credentials

Trino uses an Iceberg connector catalog file with `iceberg.catalog.type=rest` and REST-specific properties; Flink uses a `CREATE CATALOG ... WITH ('type'='iceberg', 'catalog-type'='rest', ...)` statement; PyIceberg uses `load_catalog`; DuckDB's iceberg extension can read tables and, in recent versions, attach REST catalogs. Feature levels differ: not every engine supports every write mode, format v3, or row-level deletes.

blocks.text: 24.6 Who owns writes

Atomic commits make concurrent writers *safe*, not *sensible*. Decide ownership per table: usually one pipeline (or one engine) writes, others read. Where several must write, give them disjoint partitions or operations (one appends, one compacts) and test conflict behaviour. Maintenance jobs (chapter 25) are writers too and must be included in this plan.

blocks.title: Three engines, one catalog
blocks.text: A retailer lands CDC with Flink into Iceberg tables registered in a Polaris-based catalog. Spark jobs build silver and gold tables nightly and run compaction. Analysts use Trino; finance reads gold tables from Snowflake through a catalog integration.
items: Flink owns writes to bronze; Spark owns silver and gold; Trino and Snowflake are read-only by grant, not by convention.
Credential vending means no engine holds standing bucket credentials.
Compaction on bronze runs in Spark and is scheduled to avoid the Flink commit cadence colliding with large rewrites.

blocks.title: Pick a catalog strategy
blocks.text: Your company runs Spark on AWS, Trino for analysts, and wants Snowflake to query the same tables. Security requires table-level permissions and no long-lived bucket credentials in compute clusters. Compare Glue, a self-hosted Polaris and a managed REST catalog, including migration path, who operates it, and which engine is allowed to commit to which tables.
hints: Which options support credential vending today for all three engines?
What happens to existing Glue-registered tables in each option?
Where do audit logs of reads and commits come from?

items: The catalog maps table names to the current metadata file and makes commits atomic.
One table must have exactly one catalog that accepts commits.
The REST spec decouples engines from catalog backends; the server checks requirements and applies updates.
Credential vending moves authorization from bucket IAM to the catalog, with short-lived scoped credentials.
Polaris, Open Catalog, Nessie, Unity Catalog and cloud catalogs differ in governance, multi-table semantics and engine support.
Multi-engine access needs an explicit write-ownership plan, including maintenance jobs.

blocks.q: Two catalogs both register the same Iceberg table and both accept commits. What is the likely outcome?
options: Nothing; metadata files make catalogs interchangeable
Each catalog advances its own pointer, so the table forks and commits through one catalog are invisible through the other
The second catalog becomes read-only automatically
Commits are replicated automatically between the catalogs
blocks.explain: Each catalog holds its own pointer and accepts swaps independently, so histories diverge. Metadata files are shared, but the current pointer is not.

blocks.q: In the REST catalog protocol, where does the compare-and-swap for a commit happen?
options: In the catalog server, which checks the commit's requirements before applying its updates
In object storage, via conditional PUT
In the engine, by renaming the metadata file
In each reader, which picks the newest metadata file it finds
blocks.explain: Clients send requirements and updates; the server validates and applies them atomically. That is what lets it also enforce permissions and audit commits.

options: The catalog copies data into its own storage
Data files are encrypted with catalog-managed keys
Engines receive short-lived storage credentials scoped to a table after the catalog authorizes the request
Engines no longer need to authenticate to the catalog
blocks.explain: Vending makes the catalog the authorization point: it checks table privileges and issues narrow, temporary credentials. Engines still authenticate to the catalog; no data is copied.

blocks.q: Which capability is the distinguishing feature of Nessie compared with a plain REST catalog?
options: Git-like branches and commits spanning multiple tables
blocks.explain: Nessie versions the whole catalog, so changes across several tables can be committed and merged together. Iceberg tables themselves already support hidden partitioning and per-table branches.
